subject: combined-science

items.q: Which statement best describes an electromagnetic wave?
items.correct: A transverse wave that transfers energy from source to absorber
items.misconception: A longitudinal wave that transfers energy to an absorber
items.why: Sound is usually the first wave studied in detail, and 'spreads out from a source' is remembered as the defining feature rather than the direction of the oscillation. Spreading out from a source says nothing about the type of wave. All electromagnetic waves are transverse; sound is the longitudinal one.
items.random_wrong: A transverse wave that transfers matter to an absorber

items.q: A transmitter sends radio waves to a distant aerial. What is transferred, and in which direction?
items.correct: Energy, from the source of the wave to the absorber
items.misconception: Particles of matter, from the transmitter to the aerial
items.why: Everyday transfers involve something moving — post, water through a pipe — so the student looks for a substance making the journey. The wave transfers energy only. A radio aerial gains energy from a transmitter but gains no material from it.
items.random_wrong: Energy, carried along by the air between them

items.q: How do the speeds of radio waves, visible light and gamma rays compare in a vacuum?
items.correct: All of them travel at the same velocity in a vacuum
items.misconception: Gamma rays are fastest because they carry the most energy
items.why: Energy, frequency and speed are collapsed into one idea of 'how powerful the wave is'. Danger is also read as speed. Speed in a vacuum is the same for every group. What changes across the spectrum is wavelength and frequency, and it is the high frequency, not high speed, that makes gamma rays hazardous.
items.random_wrong: Radio waves are fastest because their wavelength is longest

items.q: The electromagnetic spectrum is described as continuous. What does this mean?
items.correct: There are no gaps between one group and the next
items.misconception: It is made of seven separate waves with gaps between them
items.why: The spectrum is nearly always drawn as seven labelled boxes, and the boxes are taken to be seven distinct wave types. The boxes are labels for regions of one continuous range. The boundaries are conventions: there is a wavelength at which infrared merges into microwave with nothing missing in between.
items.random_wrong: It jumps in seven fixed steps like rungs on a ladder

items.q: Which list gives the electromagnetic groups in order from longest wavelength to shortest?
items.correct: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
items.misconception: Radio, microwave, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, X-rays, gamma
items.why: The prefixes are not connected to the colours they name: 'infra-red' means below red and 'ultra-violet' means beyond violet, but neither is obvious from the word alone. Use the colour in the name. Infrared sits next to red, at longer wavelength; ultraviolet sits next to violet, at shorter wavelength.
items.random_wrong: Gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio

items.q: Moving across the spectrum from radio waves towards gamma rays, what happens to wavelength and frequency?
items.misconception: Wavelength and frequency both increase together
items.why: Both are described as measures of the wave, and 'bigger wave' is treated as bigger in every respect at once. They are inversely related. Going from radio to gamma the wavelength gets shorter while the frequency gets higher — which is why the specification gives the same order twice, long to short wavelength or low to high frequency.
items.random_wrong: Wavelength rises while the frequency falls

items.q: A hot radiator emits infrared radiation. Why can a person in the room not see it?
items.correct: Our eyes only detect visible light, not infrared
items.misconception: The radiator is not hot enough to glow visibly yet
items.why: A glowing hot object really is visible, but that is the visible light it emits; thermal images are also shown in false colour, which suggests the eye is seeing the infrared itself. The camera detects infrared and converts it into a visible image for us. Without the camera there is nothing to see, because the eye responds only to the visible part of the spectrum.
items.random_wrong: The eye can see infrared, but only in a dark room

items.q: Which of these is the best example of energy being transferred by an electromagnetic wave?
items.correct: Sunlight warming a dark road surface
items.misconception: A loudspeaker making the nearby air vibrate
items.why: The name of the device and the output the student hears are the same word, and the invisible stage in between is not observed. The transmitter sends electromagnetic radio waves to the aerial. The loudspeaker then uses that energy to make sound waves in the air, which is a separate step.
items.random_wrong: Warm air rising above a heater in a room

items.q: Do electromagnetic waves need air, or some other substance, to travel through?
items.correct: No. They travel through a vacuum (space) as well as through air.
items.misconception: A wave must have something to travel through, so light must be carried by air — there must be very thin air out in space carrying sunlight to us.
items.why: Sound, water waves and waves on a rope are all met before light, and every one of them needs a substance. The rule 'a wave needs a medium' is then over-generalised. Electromagnetic waves are the exception: they need no medium. Sunlight, infrared and ultraviolet cross millions of kilometres of empty space to reach the Earth, which they could not do if a substance were required.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Within visible light, which colour has the longest wavelength?
items.correct: Red. The visible group runs from red at the long-wavelength end to violet at the short-wavelength end.
items.misconception: Violet has the longest wavelength because it is the strongest, deepest-looking colour.
items.why: The order of the colours is memorised as a rainbow list without attaching it to wavelength, and appearance is used instead. The specification writes the group as 'visible light (red to violet)', which is the long-to-short wavelength order. Violet is nearest to ultraviolet, the shorter-wavelength side.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is every transfer of energy that warms something a transfer by electromagnetic waves?
items.correct: No. Conduction and convection move energy using particles of matter, not waves.
items.misconception: Anything that warms up must have been warmed by radiation, so a spoon in hot tea is an example of energy transfer by an electromagnetic wave.
items.why: Heating is filed under one heading, so the three transfer processes are not separated when an example is judged. Ask whether a wave crossed a gap. Sunlight warming a road crosses empty space, so it is electromagnetic; a spoon warms by touching the tea, which is conduction.
